  • The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft introduced back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu.
  • But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 mission, due to the spacecraft suffering trouble with its ion thrusters.

The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft introduced back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu. Since delivering the samples to Earth in December 2020 via a reentry capsule, the main spacecraft has been conducting an extended mission of exploration and in July made a super-close flyby of the two-headed asteroid Torifune.

But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end. The spacecraft was scheduled to rendezvous with, and attempt to land on, the tiny, 36-foot-wide (11 meters) near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, but trouble with the aging spacecraft's engines has forced a change of blueprint.

But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end. The spacecraft was scheduled to rendezvous with, and attempt to land on, the tiny, 36-foot-wide (11 meters) near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, but trouble with the aging spacecraft's engines has forced a change of plan.

In a recent development, the spacecraft will instead target 2015 BM510, another tiny asteroid. And there will be no landing: Hayabusa2 is scheduled to make a high-speed flyby of the near-Earth object in April 2028.

The decision was announced at a Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) press conference on Tuesday (Nov. 17), a day after a Cabinet Office space policy subcommittee meeting. The final functioning thruster out of Hayabusa2's four ion engines suffered a malfunction in mid-August, according to JAXA officials, while a sensor detected unexpected erosion of the spacecraft's surface during its long voyage in space.

"The deterioration of the onboard equipment ... is becoming increasingly evident," Japan Times quoted Yuya Mimasu, team leader of the extended mission, as saying.

Sources indicate that despite losing the opportunity to land on KY26, the Hayabusa2 mission has been a huge success for JAXA, and the new direction promises its own intrigues. Asteroid 2015 BM510 has already attracted interest; it's the primary target of a proposal for the European Space Agency's mini-Fast mission series. Scientists describe the body as a D-type asteroid, meaning it's thought to be organic-rich and comet-like, and may have originated in the outer solar system.

Around the same time as Hayabusa2 conducts its high-speed flyby in April 2028, JAXA is also scheduled to launch its next asteroid mission, Destiny+. Launching along with ESA's Ramses mission to study Apophis, Destiny+ will first make a flyby of the infamous asteroid ahead of its very close approach to Earth in 2029 before heading to asteroid 3200 Phaethon, the parent body of the Geminid meteor shower.

Recent findings suggest that I don't usually bring a chair backpacking—I just sit on the ground. But for some reason, I do love a chair when I'm bike packing, which is where I've used this Nemo the most. It's quite pricey, but it's very light and packs down to a tiny package. The genius part of this chair is that the cover is also a mat that keeps it from sinking into soft ground.

The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI-brand gear is the firm's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works quite well and has generated some really great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example of that. It's not as nice as the Nemo above—it does wobble a bit, side to side, when you move—but it's still comfortable and half the price.

It has been revealed that this camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is a bit big, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.

I sincerely hope you never have any need for one of these Sea to Summit bug head nets, but if you do, boy do you. I once did not have one and tried to go backpacking in Michigan’s UP in early May. I lasted about two hours. When I got home, I bought one of these and … still haven't ventured back to that marshy bog of a hike. But I could, and possibly even retain some of my sanity thanks to this thing.

Industry observers note that what I said about the chair above goes for this day pack as well; it's an excellent value, especially on sale. I was surprised by how comfortable this thing is, especially because, to look at it, the straps are very lightweight and there's almost no padding. It still managed to carry loads up to 10 pounds without straining my shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. The Flash 22 is made of 70-denier recycled ripstop nylon, which is on the lighter side, but mine has held up well, even coming through some rough canyon hikes in Utah without any more than mud stains.

In a recent development, these two pots are my go-to cooking vessels for larger group meals. I find they're just about perfect for boiling up enough water to rehydrate four servings. I don't take the bowls and silverware into the backcountry, but they're handy for camping.

Sources indicate that sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's new inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

In a recent development, the Stash is our favorite all-in-one backcountry cook system. The heat diffuser design is what speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I was only able to match indoors in still air), but the real appeal here to me is the way this kit all packs down into itself. For weekend trips, this is the simplest system I've tested when it comes to cooking for two.

Jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.

Sources indicate that these dry bags from Sea to Summit have double-stitched, tape-sealed seams that have held up well over the years. I also really like the external lash loops that make it easy to strap to anything with a tie-down anchor.

I like these dry bags for organizing things in my pack. They're not dry bags in the sense that you can submerge them and your gear will be fine, but the 30D silnylon with PCF-free DWR easily sheds a little rain. And they make finding your stuff easy. I put all my cooking gear in a red bag (red for fire), all my water-filtering stuff in a blue bag for, wait for it, water—and so on. I find the 3- and 5-liter bags the most useful, but you can get all the way up to 35L.

Recent findings suggest that I've noticed that, when trying to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter-weight backpack, people then struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which takes my favorite sleeping bag (the Sea to Summit Spark above) and smashes it down to about half the size of the included stuff sack. You can do the same thing to clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino to some extent, to free up more room in your pack.

It has been revealed that REI’s Significant Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.

Once upon a time, in a galaxy far, far away, I traveled around Southeast Asia with an early version of this Osprey pack, living out of it for almost a year. It stood up well to the abuse of overland travel—more than once, I watched a bus driver tie it to the roof of a bus by cinching it down with a rope, pulling with all his weight right down the middle of my pack, like a cheese cutter. The Farpoint survived, and my gear inside did as well, thanks in part to the thickly padded sides, which provide considerable extra cushioning.

Latest Update: Robins ‘aims for the stars’ as Stoke dream of Premier League return

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Championship’s form side climbed to second after holding on resiliently with 10 men to knock Birmingham off the summit.
  • Recent findings suggest that there have been false dawns before.
  • According to recent reports, experience has taught the benefit of pragmatism, so no one will be getting ahead of themselves just yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Championship’s form side climbed to second after holding on resiliently with 10 men to knock Birmingham off the summit.

Recent findings suggest that there have been false dawns before. Plenty of them. This time last year, with Christmas on the near horizon, Stoke sat second in the Championship table and were beginning to wonder whether they might allow themselves to dream. So hopeless was their subsequent run that by the onset of spring they were forced to consider a potential relegation fight.

According to recent reports, experience has taught the benefit of pragmatism, so no one will be getting ahead of themselves just yet. But this weekend was supposed to be the major test for Mark Robins’s team and few considered they would pass it quite so resoundingly.

Sources indicate that facing a Birmingham side who arrived top of the table and with firmly held Premier League ambitions, Stoke dominated for an hour, the hitherto goal-shy George Hirst earning a well-deserved lead to send a bumper crowd into raptures. The hand-wringing that then followed Luca Bombino’s sending-off with half an hour remaining made the victory that followed all the sweeter. The 10 men of Stoke were superb. It was no surprise that it took considerable time to convince those in the stands to depart for home after the final whistle.

You see, it is not just that Stoke are second in the table, kept off top spot by goal difference. It is not even that they are undoubtedly the Championship’s form side, with just one defeat in their past 13 games. It is the whole feeling around the place; the resilience Robins has developed, and the belief that they can take on the significant guns and beat them.

According to recent reports, “We are a work in progress, but today was that step in quality against different opponents. A step up in class,” said Robins. “I thought we were really, really good. The intensity, bravery and the intent that we showed was everything that we asked for.

Sources indicate that “And, on the back of that, you’ve got the support that are absolutely right behind us. They trust the players. That is a really good feeling. It’s a great feeling for the players. It’s a heady mix, really.”.

Eight years have passed since Stoke were last in the top flight; eight years spent as the Championship equivalent of a sea sponge, doing the bare minimum to survive and letting defeats wash over them while remaining resolutely attached to the rocks of the bottom half of the table. During that time they have ended every campaign no higher than 14th and no lower than 18th. Now, something altogether different is afoot. And this may well be the win that convinces supporters to trust their upbeat instincts.

Industry observers note that there was an unavoidable fact heading into Saturday’s game. Stoke’s four defeats this season had all come when tasked with opponents fighting at the top end of the table in Swansea, Southampton, Wolves and Middlesbrough. They had shown themselves capable against much of the division, but a failure to deliver against another Championship heavyweight would have raised legitimate questions about their realistic aspirations.

Sources indicate that the three August defeats at the start of the campaign preceded the departure of their best player, Sorba Thomas. His replacement, Jack McGlynn, has been an inspired signing. That this victory came without the talismanic figure of Ethan Galbraith, who was absent through illness, is considerable.

As well as switching to a three-man defence following those season-opening losses, a key factor in their upturn has been the restoration of a touch of old-school Stoke; a physicality that was frequently evident on a cold Saturday afternoon.

Bobby Madley, the referee, did not always take kindly to such an approach – to the indignation of the home crowd, who frequently made their feelings clear – but there was no complaint over Bombino’s sending-off for a second yellow after a rash challenge that left him head in hands before the card had even been shown. Tears followed on his slow trudge towards the tunnel, but he need not have worried, with Birmingham barely threatening thereafter.

Given just five points separate the top eight in the Championship table, it would come as no great shock to see Stoke drop off at some point. They do not have the financial benefit of recent Premier League parachute payments or major-spending owners, they are not prolific goalscorers, and a look at their expected goals and expected points tallies demonstrates them firmly in the bottom half of the table. But they are finding ways to win and if McGlynn has a habit of scoring from unexpectedly long distances, perhaps it is because he is good at it.

Before this weekend, Robins had revealed that a top-eight finish was the pre-season target. “You aim for the stars and hopefully you land trying to grab hold of one,” he had mentioned, rather poetically.

If promotion is a “P” they dare not yet speak of, another one – playoffs – is becoming an increasingly realistic proposition. No more sticking to a rock. Swim free and prosper.

#93614. Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1297 w)

Euclid discovers ancient cosmic beacons from the dawn of time, shining like a trillion suns

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed.
  • It has been revealed that quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos.
  • It has been revealed that astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope has discovered 31 exceptionally ancient quasars, including two that have set new records as the earliest ever observed. These brilliant galactic centers, powered by enormous black holes, were already radiating as much light as a trillion Suns when the Universe was only 670 million years old, about 5% of its present age.

It has been revealed that quasars are among the brightest objects in the cosmos. They appear during a relatively short period in a galaxy's history when huge quantities of gas and other material spiral toward its central supermassive black hole. This process releases extraordinary amounts of energy, causing the galaxy's core to shine hundreds or even thousands of times more brightly than the rest of the galaxy combined.

It has been revealed that astronomers have spent decades searching for quasars from the Universe's earliest years because they offer valuable clues about the formation of the first galaxies and supermassive black holes. Finding them, however, is extremely challenging. Few galaxies had grown large enough to host such objects at that early stage, and the light reaching us today is incredibly faint. These distant sources can also be difficult to distinguish from stars much closer to Earth.

Sources indicate that released in 2023, Euclid is transforming that search. Its ability to survey enormous regions of the sky and detect faint objects has already produced an unprecedented collection of 31 quasars from the early Universe, including some dating back to when the cosmos was just 5% of its current age.

"These early quasars date back to the Universe's infancy," says Daming Yang of Leiden University in the Netherlands, lead author of the Euclid discovery paper. "By finding and studying them, we can better understand how these enormous systems formed and grew so quickly - one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics.".

Euclid Reveals a Hidden Population of Ancient Quasars.

Until now, astronomers had identified only a small fraction of the quasars that existed during the Universe's earliest period. Most known examples were exceptionally luminous objects that stood out because they were easier to detect. This limited sample made it difficult to understand the broader population and how these powerful systems developed.

Euclid is changing that picture by identifying not only the brightest quasars but also much fainter examples that previous searches struggled to find. Its discoveries are providing scientists with a far more representative view of the ancient quasar population, opening the door to more detailed studies of these early cosmic objects.

In a recent development, "Euclid is a true game-changer," adds Daming. "Before, we could only find a handful of the very brightest ancient quasars, but Euclid lets us search far more efficiently across huge areas of sky to capture much fainter light. It's a unique tool for quasar hunting.".

It has been revealed that among the 31 newly identified quasars, 12 have a redshift of 7 or greater. Redshift describes how light is stretched as the Universe expands and helps astronomers determine how far away an object is and how far back in cosmic history its light originated. A redshift of at least 7 places these quasars within the Universe's first 770 million years.

Two Record-Breaking Quasars From Cosmic Dawn.

Two objects stand out as particularly extraordinary. The most ancient, EUCL J172902.75+641018.1, has a redshift of 7.77, while EUCL J125308.55+705432.3 has a redshift of 7.69. Both are located just over 13 billion light-years from Earth and were already shining within the first 670 million years of cosmic history.

According to recent reports, these discoveries establish upcoming records for the earliest known quasars. The previous record belonged to an object discovered in 2021, which has a redshift of 7.64.

"This finding more than doubles the number of quasars we know of that are so ancient," indicates Antonio La Marca, an ESA Research Fellow in the Euclid team.

The pace of discovery is especially remarkable. Astronomers needed more than a decade to identify roughly the first 10 quasars with redshifts of 7 or higher. Euclid has already surpassed that number in just one year, demonstrating how dramatically the telescope is accelerating research into the early Universe.

Sources indicate that "The Euclid team has taken a true 'census' of quasars at the dawn of the Universe for the first time," adds Antonio. "It's a significant step towards understanding these fascinating objects on a more fundamental level.".

Ancient Black Holes Reveal Clues About the First Galaxies.

One of the newly discovered objects is already offering additional insight into conditions during the Universe's infancy. Silvia Belladitta and colleagues recently conducted a more detailed investigation of the second most ancient quasar identified by Daming and his team.

Sources indicate that their observations revealed that the quasar sits inside a galaxy filled with gas and dust where latest stars are forming at a tremendous rate. This provides an important glimpse of the environment surrounding an early supermassive black hole and could help researchers understand how the first massive galaxies evolved alongside the black holes at their centers.

These quasars also belong to a transformative chapter in cosmic history known as the epoch of reionization. During this period, the Universe emerged from a cold, dark state (the 'dark ages') as increasingly energetic radiation heated the surrounding gas and ionized it (split apart by energetic light). This fundamental transition helped establish the conditions that shaped the Universe we observe today.

In a recent development, "Ancient quasars are rare discoveries. They're interesting in themselves, but also time machines that enable us to explore the early Universe and understand how the first generation of galaxies came to be," notes ESA Euclid Project Scientist Valeria Pettorino.

How Euclid Is Transforming the Search for Cosmic Giants.

Euclid's success comes from a powerful combination of capabilities. The telescope can examine enormous portions of the sky while collecting detailed images and detecting faint infrared light from extremely distant objects. Together, these features make it exceptionally effective at finding rare sources that earlier surveys could easily miss.

Recent findings suggest that "Euclid's capabilities are unrivaled. The telescope combines a large area, depth, sharp imaging, and unique space-based infrared vision in a way that lets us pick out rare, extremely distant objects far more efficiently than before.

"And it's not just the telescope: the data processing is only possible thanks to thousands of Euclid Consortium scientists and engineers working together to deliver scientific discoveries, sifting through enormous datasets to identify rare, distant quasars that we can study further using telescopes on the ground.".

All 31 quasars were identified using observations from the Euclid Wide Survey, an ambitious project that will eventually examine more than one-third of the entire sky.

Sources indicate that although Euclid's primary mission is to investigate the dark Universe, its observations are revealing much more. By studying billions of galaxies, the telescope is helping astronomers investigate the Universe's composition, history, evolution, and vast cosmic structure. At the same time, its sweeping survey is uncovering rare ancient quasars that offer a remarkable opportunity to explore how the first galaxies and giant black holes emerged.

As Euclid continues mapping the cosmos, astronomers expect its growing collection of distant quasars to provide newly introduced clues about one of astrophysics' most enduring questions: how supermassive black holes became so enormous in such a remarkably short time after the Big Bang.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nicole Richie has a simple solution for her beauty needs.

The Simple Life alum revealed that her and husband Joel Madden’s 18-year-old daughter Harlow Kate Madden has become her go-to makeup artist, as the teen is even more skilled than she is in that particular area.

“I would say that she has surpassed me,” Richie told People in an interview published Nov. 19. “She’s so good. I actually am not very good at doing my own makeup. She is a whole different animal.”.

And the 45-year-old knows exactly how her daughter—who chooses to go by her middle name Kate—got so good at glowing up her family.

“She grew up watching YouTube tutorials,” Richie explained, “and she’s so well-versed in makeup and contour and highlighting and just all the things.”.

“If I ever need my makeup done at home, I’m going to her,” the House of Harlow founder added. “It’s not me doing it ... She kills a cat-eye.”.

Of course, Kate will soon be showing off more of her talents as she officially builds the foundation for a modeling career after signing with The Lions Management.

“I’ve always dreamed of modeling, so getting to start this next chapter with The Lions is incredibly exciting,” Kate shared in a Nov. 20 statement to Women’s Wear Daily. “Fashion has always been a way for me to express myself, and I can’t wait to explore that in a whole new way.”.

She added, “I’m looking forward to learning, growing, meeting new people, and seeing where this journey takes me.”.

Kate made her modeling debut alongside her mom for Balenciaga’s recent campaign celebrating the 25th anniversary of their Le City handbag, a style Richie was particularly fond of in the early 2000s.

And Madden—who also shares son Sparrow James Midnight, 17, with Richie—was particularly thrilled to see his daughter achieving her dream.

Sources indicate that the Good Charlotte frontman reposted Kate’s modeling announcement to his Instagram Stories Nov. 20, captioning it with three red heart emojis and writing in all caps, “KATE!”.

For a look at more celebrity kids who have strutted into the modeling world, keep reading.

It has been revealed that beyoncé’s nephew, whose mom is Solange Knowles, made his fashion debut April 2024 at Luar’s Fall 2024 runway. Two months later, he debuted at Paris Fashion Week for the Bluemarble Spring 2025 show.

Heidi Klum and Seal’s son made his runway debut at the Lena Erziak Haute Couture Spring-Summer 2025 Show during Paris Fashion Week in January 2025.

Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Riemann hypothesis has been a lodestar for generations of mathetmaticians.
  • In a recent development, in a year that has seen artificial intelligence reach one spectacular mathematical breakthrough after another, Anthropic has now claimed the top prize of them all: a full proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the statement that many mathematicians consider the most crucial open problem in the field.
  • The Anthropic announcement came on 20 November from Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the San Francisco, California tech giant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Riemann hypothesis has been a lodestar for generations of mathetmaticians. Credit: James Brittain/Getty.

In a recent development, in a year that has seen artificial intelligence reach one spectacular mathematical breakthrough after another, Anthropic has now claimed the top prize of them all: a full proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the statement that many mathematicians consider the most crucial open problem in the field. But on the same day as the Anthropic claim, a separate study claiming to have proven the Riemann also emerged — and this one is entirely human written.

The Anthropic announcement came on 20 November from Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the San Francisco, California tech giant. “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote, referring to Anthropic’s large language model (LLM).

“If this fully checks out, it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics,” states number theorist James Maynard, a Fields Medal winner at the University of Oxford, UK, says.

Anthropic AI ‘formalizes’ proof of Fermat’s last theorem — a milestone for mathematics.

Anthropic AI ‘formalizes’ proof of Fermat’s last theorem — a milestone for mathematics.

Hours later, Ravi Vakil, a mathematician at Stanford University in California, posted online a rival preprint to Alpöge’s, in what Vakil called a “hurried announcement.” The preprint was written by Alessandro Maria Masullo, a mathematician who received his PhD at Stanford in 2020 under the supervision of number theorist Brian Conrad. “The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people,” Vakil wrote. “Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”.

The confirmation of either or both solutions would be a spectacular bicentenary present for Bernhard Riemann, the German mathematician who was born 200 years ago this September and who formulated the problem, which addresses the distribution of prime numbers, in the mid-1800.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which has its scientific headquarters in Oxford, UK , at the turn of the twenty-first century. The institute offers a US$1 million prize to anyone who devises a solution to one of the problems, which are considered some of the most challenging in the field. Mathematicians using AI tools announced earlier this year that they had solved another Millennium problem, related to the Navier-Stokes equation.

Industry observers note that the problem has to do with the ‘Riemann ζ function’ (ζ is the Greek letter zeta), which encodes the randomness properties of the prime numbers. Riemann discovered that the distribution of primes is encoded in the ζ function’s ‘zeroes.’ These are points, denoted by z, on a plane satisfying the equation ζ(z) = 0.

Riemann conjectured that apart from some obvious but uninteresting cases, all such solutions had to lie on a certain vertical line in the plane. If this were true, he demonstrated, it would imply that prime numbers are scattered among all whole numbers in a way that is essentially as random as it could be.

In a recent development, alpöge’s 4-page document includes a sketch of the proof. But Andrew Granville, a number theorist at the University of Montreal in Canada, claims that Alpöge should have taken the time to prepare a clearer write-up before making the announcement, which came just days after Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO). The IPO initially valued the company at US$1.5 trillion, but the company’s valuation dropped on 19 November.

According to recent reports, “What he released is garbled,” Granville claims of Alpöge’s document. Granville cites the downturn in the tech giant’s stock value as the reason for the timing of the proof’s release.

“There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false,” Alpöge wrote in the document.

Anthropic did not respond immediately to Nature’s request for comment.

In a recent development, tristan Buckmaster, a mathematician at Latest York University who collaborated with Alpöge on a separate project regarding the Navier-Stokes equation, states that Alpöge deserves a lot of credit for developing techniques to produce mathematical results using LLMs. “Levent himself built this amazing setup to do math”. He adds that Alpöge, who is himself a number theorist on leave from Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been working relentlessly for months on this and other problems, hardly ever getting any sleep.

‘The job description is changing’: mathematician Terence Tao on the rise of AI.

‘The job description is changing’: mathematician Terence Tao on the rise of AI.

“I suspect that the proof will turn out to be correct,” Maynard says of the Alpöge announcement, even though it is now in the form of incomprehensible code in the Lean programming language.

“At the moment, it apparently is crazily complicated. It’s going to take a long time for mathematicians to digest,” states Buckmaster. Maynard agrees, but he adds, “assuming we do get the corresponding understanding, this will surely be viewed as one of the absolute pinnacles of mathematical results”.

  • In a recent development, according to Anthropic, the first conundrum Claude was able to solve involved the concept of heating up a hypothetical universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At a time when Anthropic is vacuuming up stock market money, the AI company has made a pretty grandiose claim about its Claude chatbot's scientific capabilities.

Sources indicate that the San Francisco-based artificial intelligence firm published a lengthy blog post this week claiming that its Claude Fable 5.2 model had made some progress on figuring out two long-standing mysteries surrounding black holes. The post goes into an incredible amount of scientific detail that might fly over your head (as much of it did mine), but I'll try my best to summarize it in plain English.

In a recent development, according to Anthropic, the first conundrum Claude was able to solve involved the concept of heating up a hypothetical universe. When the universe reaches a certain temperature, it would form a black hole through a sudden "phase transition," as initially described by Stephen Hawking and Don Page in 1983. Hawking and Page's findings concerned only a vast universe described by general relativity, while this theoretical universe is much smaller and might work differently.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Industry observers note that it turns out, as Claude found, that the phase transition is also abrupt in a smaller universe. As Anthropic explained, this implies that "black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.".

Recent findings suggest that as for the second finding, it revolves around another theoretical universe made up of two dimensions instead of three. In this universe, physicists have spent years trying to figure out how heavy the lightest possible black hole could be using a technique called "bootstrapping," in which the ceiling for the lightest black hole gets lowered each time a theory breaks it. Anthropic claimed that Claude Fable 5.2 was able to notice a pattern that physicists had missed in their calculations and use it to "calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered.".

As Anthropic was quick to point out in the blog post, these findings do not apply to our universe or have any practical application but could give us an idea of how relativity and quantum mechanics work together. It's also worth noting that these findings were released alongside Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO, AKA a time when Anthropic wants as much public money as possible.

Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
  • This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.
  • According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

Recent findings suggest that his two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

According to recent reports, in a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible.".

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers.".

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," remarked political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach.".

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

Sources indicate that "In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.

Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside, where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed team fought back commendably to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance. At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and subtle tactical rejig suggested he is no mug after all.

It left Arsenal – who lost their outstanding goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League, six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City, and Arteta with a face like thunder.

Sources indicate that just last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’s former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players. Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending about £275m this summer, they have struggled to replace last season’s departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.

In a recent development, that reality perhaps left Howe’s successor – who arrived just before the start of the season – making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here. Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were close-season signings.

The other five upcoming faces were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man matchday squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given Bamba and Toure cost a combined £78.5m, their omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to bench González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tag.

It has been revealed that meanwhile the jury remains out on Hornicek. The Czech international has made some excellent saves this season but, initially here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved after hesitating too long as the impressive Kai Havertz closed in.

Jaissle’s frustration with his goalkeeper proved well apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula, isolated and even their normally imperious England left-back Lewis Hall given a thorough work out by Noni Madueke.

Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, endeavoured to slow the tempo but the red tide could only be stemmed for so long.

According to recent reports, when Havertz dispossessed Hall after the latter miscontrolled a long ball, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated, pass across to the on-rushing Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance and unleashed a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, past Hornicek.

• Arsenal ended a 21-game run of Premier League games without a draw (W18 D3) since a 2-2 draw with Wolves back in February.

• Since the start of last season, all five of Newcastle’s Premier League draws at St James’ Park have been a 2-2 scoreline.

• Eberechi Eze’s opener for Arsenal (pictured) was his first Premier League goal since April, which also put the Gunners 1-0 ahead against Newcastle. Opta.

As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.

Sources indicate that with Declan Rice always available to reinforce his defence and smother any flickering home attack it proved a struggle to recall Newcastle making a meaningful attacking touch inside Arsenal’s box. Fans stationed near the home dugouts told Jaissle what they thought of it all.

According to recent reports, arsenal’s pressing was initially so good that Newcastle were left almost incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.

Yet that seemingly ambitious vision was something Harvey Barnes proved fully capable of buying into. When, early in the second half, Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch sliced the ball in Osula’s direction and the Dane played it into Barnes’s path.

All that remained was for the left winger to take a single, steadying, touch before an assured finish left the hitherto redundant David Raya picking his shot out of the net.

Sources indicate that jaissle’s second-half introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga – all at Newcastle last season – at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy was paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.

The home side were closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team. Soon, they were ahead when a Hall corner was headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.

Sources indicate that shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring Guimarães’s exit.

Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counterattacking Ødegaard’s fine pass, dummying two defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.

Industry observers note that no matter; Jaissle had done enough to win plenty of hearts and minds. Not least the chair, Yasir al-Rumayyan, over from Riyadh to watch his first match of the season and reportedly “take the club’s temperature”.

A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.

In a recent development, the firm notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms.

You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower.

"The Starbase tower chopsticks catching their first Starship. This unique architecture was designed for full and rapid reusability, enabling repeat rolls out and landings from the same pad," SpaceX wrote in a Tuesday X post that shared the videos, a compilation of which you can see embedded above.

In a recent development, starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. Its current "V3" version stands about 408 feet (124 m) tall, and future iterations will be even larger.

It has been revealed that as SpaceX noted in Tuesday's post, the megarocket is also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first for an orbital launch system. The company looks to catch both Starship stages — Ship and the Super Heavy booster — at the launch tower, a recovery strategy designed to enable efficient inspection, refurbishment and reflight.

SpaceX planned to carry out such a double catch on this most recent test flight, Starship's 15th to date, which launched on Friday evening (Nov. 13). But Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel warning during its return to Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launch and autonomously diverted to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico.

That wasn't a huge deal for SpaceX, as it had already caught Super Heavy on three previous test flights. Snagging Ship is tougher; the upper stage returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter than the booster does.

Recent findings suggest that spaceX had not even attempted a Ship catch before Flight 15. But the firm managed to pull off the maneuver on its first try.

And Ship did some work in orbit before coming home: It deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites on Flight 15, the second batch that the manufacturer has sent to low Earth orbit. The first set was deployed on Flight 14, which rolled out on Sept. 28.

#93607. Breaking: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

Breaking: Scientists find a simple daily routine linked to less pain and depression

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize.
  • The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an key role in physical and mental well-being.
  • According to recent reports, the discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A consistent daily routine may do more for your health than you realize. Researchers at the University of Missouri have found that older adults who follow regular daily schedules tend to experience less physical pain and fewer symptoms of depression, even when they struggle to get a good night's sleep.

The findings suggest that everyday habits, such as waking up, eating meals, socializing, and going to bed at consistent times, may play an key role in physical and mental well-being. By helping the body maintain its natural internal clock, a predictable routine could offer health benefits that extend beyond improved sleep.

According to recent reports, the discovery could be especially crucial for older adults, who frequently experience sleep difficulties. According to the National Council on Aging, roughly half of adults age 60 and older report symptoms of insomnia, a condition that can make it difficult to fall asleep, stay asleep, or get restful sleep.

Daily Routines Linked to Less Pain and Depression.

To investigate the relationship between sleep, daily habits, and overall health, Eunjin Tracy, an assistant professor in the College of Education and Human Development at the University of Missouri, examined survey responses from 67 older adults. Among the participants, 37 reported experiencing insomnia.

As researchers expected, those with insomnia generally reported more physical pain and higher levels of depression than participants without the condition. However, another pattern emerged when Tracy examined their daily routines.

Participants who maintained more consistent schedules tended to report less pain and fewer depressive symptoms, regardless of their sleep quality. This suggests that keeping regular daily habits may be associated with better health even when sleep problems persist.

According to recent reports, "Regardless of sleep quality, those who reported having a regular daily routine had lower levels of physical pain and less depression compared to those without a daily routine," Tracy stated. "If we are consistent with when we wake up, eat, work or study, interact with others and go to bed, those time cues help synchronize our internal body clocks. Over the long term, that seems to be linked with improved health outcomes.".

Why Your Body's Internal Clock Matters.

One possible explanation involves the circadian rhythm, the body's natural 24-hour timing system. This internal clock helps coordinate when we feel awake or sleepy and influences numerous biological processes, including hormone activity, metabolism, and mood.

Rather than operating independently of our surroundings, the circadian system responds to signals that help it keep time. Light and darkness are especially key, but regular activities such as eating, working, interacting with others, and sleeping can also provide timing cues.

Recent findings suggest that when these signals follow a predictable pattern, they help keep the body's biological rhythms aligned. Irregular schedules, on the other hand, can interfere with that coordination.

"When we regulate our circadian rhythm well, our bodies function well, but if it gets too distracted, our bodies don't function as well," Tracy stated.

Although the study did not establish that regular routines directly reduce pain or depression, the findings point to circadian regulation as one possible explanation for the connection.

The Hidden Effects of Social Jet Lag.

According to recent reports, even relatively small changes in daily schedules may disrupt the body's internal clock. One common example is social jet lag, which occurs when a person's sleep schedule shifts between workdays and days off.

Industry observers note that someone who wakes up early throughout the week but stays up late and sleeps in on weekends may experience this mismatch. The resulting disruption resembles some of the effects of traveling across time zones, even though the person has never left home.

Tracy suggests that maintaining reasonably consistent schedules throughout the entire week, including weekends, may help limit these disruptions and support healthier circadian rhythms.

"As someone who wakes up and goes to bed at the same time every day, I think a daily routine can be helpful for people of all ages across their lifespan," Tracy stated. "There is growing awareness about the concept of social jet lag -- waking up and going to bed at different times on weekends compared to weekdays -- and the disruptions it causes to our circadian rhythm, so hopefully this research helps more people consider the health benefits of a daily routine. Since one-third of our lives will be spent sleeping, I think health and well-being research should be looked at holistically from a 24-hour perspective and not just focus on when we are awake.".

A Simple Habit With Potential Health Benefits.

The research highlights an aspect of healthy living that can be easy to overlook. While getting enough quality sleep remains important, the consistency of activities throughout the day may also be connected to how people feel physically and emotionally.

Because the study relied on survey data from a relatively small group of older adults, it cannot prove that adopting a regular routine will relieve pain or depression. Larger studies would be needed to establish whether changing daily schedules directly improves these outcomes.

Still, the findings suggest that a predictable daily routine may be a useful component of a broader approach to health, particularly for people experiencing insomnia.

For older adults and potentially people of other ages, simple habits such as maintaining regular waking times, eating meals on a consistent schedule, and limiting major changes in weekend sleep patterns may help support the body's natural rhythms.

The study, "Behavioral-social rhythms and insomnia symptoms: associations with pain, body mass index, and depressive symptoms among older adults," was published in the Journal of Behavioral Medicine.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Evanilson strikes again as Bournemouth see off Forest.

"We have to stick together and face reality.".

That is how Bournemouth manager Marco Rose responded after his side had dropped into the Premier League relegation zone with a 5-1 defeat by Chelsea.

Six weeks on, it is an entirely different story.

The Cherries are up to fourth in the top flight, having clinched a club record ninth successive win in all competitions - with five in the league.

It is a far cry from that thumping defeat at Stamford Bridge, which left Rose without a victory in his first six Premier League matches in charge.

Bournemouth earned just three points from those six games (draws against Everton, Newcastle and Brentford - when the Cherries squandered winning positions) and fans may have been fearing the worst.

From the outside looking in, it seemed as though the appointment of Rose might not deliver the fortunes that had been expected.

The 50-year-old, who accepted the unenviable task of succeeding Andoni Iraola, called for his side to take "responsibility" after the defeat by Chelsea.

Recent findings suggest that "Three points after six games, we need a reaction. Everyone has to take responsibility to do better," stated Rose at the time.

According to recent reports, "We knew it was going to be a demanding season. We have to stick together and face reality. The reality is we have three points after six games.".

The Cherries have not only responded to Rose's rallying cry, they have exceeded all expectations.

Those nine straight wins include five in the league - and his side are now only four points behind second-placed Brighton.

After easing to a 2-0 victory against Nottingham Forest on Saturday, Rose mentioned: "We don't think about records, we just think about the next game.

Sources indicate that "We took the right approach. We knew it would be tough and we would have to stay patient, and that's what we did. It was a top performance and a deserved win.".

Bournemouth's nine-game winning streak is a club record - beating two separate runs of eight in 1998-99 and 2012-13.

Since arriving in England in July, Rose has come across as a composed presence, regardless of Bournemouth's results.

However, the former Borussia Dortmund and RB Leipzig manager was unable to hide his delight at his side's record-breaking victory against Forest.

Shortly after the full-time whistle sounded at the Vitality Stadium, Rose unleashed a series of celebratory fist pumps in front of the delighted home fans.

It was arguably the first time Rose had let down his guard since arriving on the South Coast four months ago - and who could blame him, given the significance of the result?

It is the first time in the club's history they have won five consecutive Premier League matches.

The prospect of securing European football for a second consecutive season is growing by the week.

In addition to wins over Sunderland, Manchester United, Leeds, Ipswich and Nottingham Forest in the Premier League, Bournemouth have beaten AC Milan in the Europa League and Aston Villa in the League Cup.

Their remarkable run of nine wins across all competitions surpasses their previous record of eight, achieved in both the 1998-99 and 2012-13 seasons.

Bournemouth are at the moment also second in the Europa League league phase and are one of only three teams to have won all four of their matches so far.

"Tonight I will smile, but not just because of the table - because we win," Rose told Match of the Day.

Meanwhile, Justin Kluivert - who scored Bournemouth's second goal against Forest - urged his team-mates to remain "humble" and "not settle for less" before upcoming matches against Celta Vigo and Fulham.

'I'll call him' - Justin Kluivert happy he's scored same week as dad Patrick.

One of the main reasons behind Bournemouth's upturn in form has been the hot streak forward Evanilson is currently enjoying.

After failing to find the back of the net in his first five appearances of the season, the Brazilian became the first player in club history to score in six consecutive Premier League matches when he broke the deadlock against Forest.

Since joining the Cherries in a club record deal from Porto in August 2024, the 27-year-old has struggled for consistency.

In his first season in England, Evanilson managed 10 goals and five assists in 31 league appearances.

Last season, though, was less productive for the forward, who managed only six goals and three assists in 36 top-flight appearances.

By scoring against Forest, Evanilson has already matched his return from the previous campaign.

In a recent development, "He is lovely, he works hard and his quality does the rest," noted Kluivert. "I am happy he has been scoring, and working hard for the team.".

Industry observers note that it is not only goals that Evanilson is providing for his side this season. He has also proven that he is able to drop between the lines - and out wide - to allow Bournemouth to be a fluid side in transition.

That was evident for the Cherries' second goal against Forest, when Evanilson pulled out to the left touchline and threaded the ball down the line for Marcus Tavernier to cross for the unmarked Kluivert in the centre.

It has been revealed that "The way he works for us out of possession, works as a link player and goes deep," added Rose. "The way he scores is quite impressive.".

The season has not even reached the halfway point, so no-one at Bournemouth will be getting carried away just yet.

What is possible for the Cherries this term will largely depend on what happens - or, perhaps more importantly, what does not happen - in January.

Bournemouth's impressive recent form - and that of certain individuals - is likely to attract attention from some of the biggest clubs in the Premier League when the transfer window opens in January.

Players such as Evanilson, Rayan, Alex Scott and Junior Kroupi, in particular, are likely to be the subject of interest from elsewhere.

So what should Bournemouth do if some of the Premier League's 'bigger' clubs come knocking for their crown jewels?

Should they resist the premium prices the mid-season market is likely to bring and keep hold of their star quality to preserve their own aspirations this season?

Former Manchester City and England goalkeeper Joe Hart believes the Cherries should try to keep hold of their stars to bolster their own hopes this term - insisting the "sky is the limit" for Rose's side.

"Rather than setting a specific target, like Champions League qualification, they should just enjoy what they are doing," Hart told BBC Sport.

"It is crucial they keep everyone fit and firing, given they have the extra demands of playing in Europe plus the busy Christmas period to come.

"Junior Kroupi and Alex Scott came off the bench today, and that kind of squad depth could be massive for them.

"It is all about keeping themselves in the running because a lot of teams are stumbling right now, whereas Bournemouth are really in a rich vein of form.".

The moment same-sex civil unions were legalized in Britain, the music icon and the Canadian ad exec were joined together in a Dec. 21, 2005 ceremony. They repeated the process on the exact same day nine years later once they were able to legally wed. And yet the anniversary they recognize is their unexpected meeting during a 1993 weekend dinner party at the singer's Windsor, England flat, his friend having set the guest list.Every Saturday, no matter where they are in the world, together or apart, the two pen a handwritten note to each other, by the authors' count, some 1,352 letters in all. "There's something very spiritual and real about handwriting," explains Furnish, "and the cards are a chance to reflect on the week that's passed and talk about the week that's coming up." Agreed the five-time Grammy winner, "It's part of the success, I think, of a lasting relationship. Communication is the most important thing.".

Having literally Secreted their 40-year marriage into existence ("Six months before I met him, I had these recurring dreams about this person I was going to marry,") they make sure their union has remained front-and-center even as their entire existence has shifted. "Marriage is a priority for both of us. And that means that we act on that and refocus when we've lost sight of the ball," she remarked. If the surgeon could prescribe one piece of advice, it would be to place that bond above all else. "The bottom line is this: I would do anything for her. Climb any mountain, take any bullet—in the chest, too, by the way. I might do things that justifiably make her really angry at me, but I would never let anything block me from delivering my love to her," he swore. If you appreciate how valuable marriage is to your long-term happiness, he continued, "You will never let anyone touch it.".

ABC News reporter Roberts isn't always one for chit-chat. "I don't like the check-in," she explaind. "If you're calling just to say, 'So, what's up?' no, I do not like that." Everyone's favorite TV weatherman, however, is a phone guy. And after years of chafing against his frequent calls, a pal proposed something that changed her stance. "One friend noted to me, 'Did you ever think that maybe he just feels comfortable when he hears your voice, because that tells him that all is right in the world?'" she recounted. "And I thought, 'That's very sweet. I'd never thought about it in that way. And if it means something to him, then it should mean something to me.'"Now, she said, "I have learned to take a breath and say, 'Sweetie, I've got some stuff going on, but what's going on with you? Great. I'm glad to hear from you. Got to go. Talk to you later. Love you.' That makes all the difference in the world to him, and it doesn't kill me for two minutes to be nice and sweet." They celebrated their 29th anniversary in September 2024.

It has been revealed that the building blocks for their nearly 30-year union began back in their newlywed days, when any fight—one involved the Riverdale actor throwing the talk show host's ring out the window—felt like it could be it. "Early in a marriage, it's easy to let little things become big things—whether it's financial strain or career strain or you have kids and you're sleep-deprived," espoused the LIVE With Kelly and Ryan star. "But Mark taught me to walk away and take a breath. That's when you figure out that it's not a marriage-defining moment."Some hard-earned wisdom, to be sure, but now the parents of three are reaping the benefits. "Anytime you see a couple who seems truly happy, you can bet they've gone through some crazy, crazy stuff together and they've survived," he stated. "That's something to be proud of.".

Sources indicate that she's an introvert, she stated, "maybe a step away from being a straight-up loner"; he's the ultimate extrovert "the mayor of everywhere," as he put it. She's a touch messy; he's "a little OCD" noted the Oscar winner. But, wed since 2003, they've long since learned to let the other do their thing. That's the advice the How to Get Away With Murder lead said she gives to all her soon-to-be-wed friends. "Marriage does not start when you walk down the aisle," she shared. "Your marriage starts when you look over at a person who you love more than anything, and there's something about him—just one character trait that makes you say to yourself, 'Oh man, that's going to drive me crazy. I don't know if I can deal with this.' And then the next minute you say, 'But you know what? I love him.' That's when your marriage starts.".

You don't reach the 50-year mark in any relationship by letting disagreements drag on. Any time there's a blowup, noted the Grace and Frankie star, "Usually, I'm the one who apologizes. It's not hard because I love her and can't bear for her to feel lonely for even five minutes." Even better is when she can avoid saying she's sorry to the writer altogether. Her top takeaway, she shared, "Remember, when you're angry at your partner and say something hurtful, you will be more angry at yourself later for having said hurtful things to the person you love. You'll feel angry twice. Not good for your blood pressure, and certainly not good for your relationship.".

Judges Judy Sheindlin & Jerry Sheindlin.

Few things are more on brand than former Fresh York State Supreme Court judge Jerry declaring their decades-long union works because he usually lets the Judge Judy icon win. But for his bride it's more about knowing you're not always going to like the final verdict. Their 12-year marriage dissolved in 1990 when he couldn't be the caretaker she needed following her father's death. Yet, when they got back together one year later and swiftly remarried, she had no delusions that he was suddenly going to be the type to run the household or take the lead on birthday looks. "Every relationship is different, but there is a common thread of unhappiness, and that unhappiness comes from trying to make another person different from who they are. You can try, but they're always going to resent it," she explained matter-of-factly. "I don't think you should marry anyone with the expectation of changing who they are.".

In a recent development, the Lost alum would be, well, lost without his longtime love, who he married in 1993. As he explained to E! News in April 2025, "My wife—being patient as I traipse around the world, going from job to job—she's kept our family stable. She's been fantastic.".

Calling her a "very patient woman," the actor remarked his wife and their two sons keeps him "humble no matter what's happening.".

"They shape my values," he added. "It's great to have that perspective and North Star.".

Industry News: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.
  • Recent findings suggest that “I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”.

After downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”.

It has been revealed that within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”.

According to recent reports, following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with customers sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.

X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person stated in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”.

Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, noted she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.

With social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.

Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

“It is probably at least partially a question of not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable things,” Pennington says. “This also strikes me as another example of information we don’t really need that social media can give us. There’s this data that exists at the platform level or would take a lot of effort to find out on your own, but now you can learn with the click of the button. But it doesn’t mean it is something you need to know.”.

In October, despite the seeming popularity of the feature, Meta removed an advertising campaign that promoted Muse with the promise that users could “see who unfollowed you each week,” Business Insider reported.

When WIRED asked about the reasoning behind Meta’s decision to remove the ad, the tech giant did not respond to a request for comment.

According to recent reports, but Muse’s capabilities aren’t just being employed to even scores. Some people are using the assistant to streamline feeds that have become extremely cluttered over the years.

Sources indicate that elizabeth Brooks is a self-proclaimed “sweeper”—the term for a hobbyist who routinely enters sweepstakes and promotional contests—who, over the course of 10 years, had followed various accounts offering giveaways. Recently, she started prompting the assistant to bring her five profile links every few hours, no more than six times a day, for her to manually unfollow one by one. “Your following list can finally work for you instead of the other way around,” she wrote on Facebook.

Roberts, who joined Instagram in high school 15 years ago and calls the platform “my app of choice,” says people are becoming more intentional about their digital relationships and who they let into their online lives. But he doesn’t plan on letting Muse make any more decisions about his social life, he says.

“Unfollowing is where I draw the line.”.

#93602. A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
